title: 1 · I want, I can
intro: We'll build real sentences from two little engine words — no memorising lists. Say each answer out loud before you reveal it.

steps.teach: אני (ani) = I. רוצה (rotze) = want. Just put them side by side.
Add an infinitive straight on. לבוא (lavo) = to come.
יכול (yachol) = can / able.
לא (lo) = not. It sits right before the verb.
steps.answer: אני לא יכול לבוא  (ani lo yachol lavo)

steps.teach: לישון (lishon) = to sleep.

steps.answer: אני לא רוצה לישון  (ani lo rotze lishon)

title: 2 · You, and asking
intro: Same engine, new pieces. To ask a yes/no question in Hebrew you keep the same word order and just raise your tone.

steps.teach: אתה (ata) = you (to a man). Word order stays the same to ask.
צריך (tzarich) = need / have to. ללכת (lalechet) = to go.
לעזור (la'azor) = to help.

steps.answer: אני לא רוצה לעזור  (ani lo rotze la'azor)

title: 3 · the, and, in
intro: The smallest words in Hebrew aren't words at all — they're single letters glued to the front of the next word. Master these and whole sentences open up.

steps.teach: ה (ha) glued on = "the". בית (bayit) = house.
ב (be) glued on = "in". Before "the", be + ha fuses to "ba".
ו (ve) glued on = "and". קפה (kafe) = coffee, מים (mayim) = water.
A definite object takes את (et) in front of it.
steps.answer: אני רוצה את הקפה  (ani rotze et ha-kafe)

title: 4 · Speaking as yourself: he says, she says
intro: This is the pattern Hebrew is built on, and it catches every English speaker. In the present tense the verb changes with the gender of whoever is speaking — so the very first sentence you say about yourself is already gendered.

steps.teach: "ani rotze" = I want, said by a man.
A woman says rotza. Same letters in writing; different word out loud.
It's every present-tense verb, not just this one. "I understand" = mevin / mevina.
And adjectives about yourself do the same. ayef / ayefa = tired.
"You" is gendered too: ata to a man, at to a woman. There's no neutral option.
The relief: in the past tense, "I" isn't gendered at all.

title: 5 · Having things without a verb for it
intro: Hebrew has no verb "to have". It says there-is-to-me instead, and once you see the shape you get the whole family of these for free.

steps.teach: "yesh" = there is. "li" = to me.
"ein" is the negative of yesh.
The ending changes for the person: lecha to a man, lach to a woman.
steps.prompt: Do you have time? (to a man)
Do you have time? (to a woman)

steps.teach: lo = to him, la = to her.
And yesh/ein work on their own for "there is" and "there isn't".

title: 6 · The word with no translation: את
intro: One small word does a job English simply doesn't have. It isn't optional, it means nothing on its own, and leaving it out is the clearest sign of a foreigner.

steps.teach: "et" goes before a definite object — a specific thing the verb acts on. It has no English equivalent at all.
No "et" when the object is indefinite. Just a film, not the film.
Names count as definite, so they take it too.
steps.hint: makira if a woman is speaking

steps.teach: So does "this", when it's the thing being acted on.
steps.prompt: How do you say this in Hebrew?

steps.teach: It merges with pronouns: et + you becomes otcha / otach.

steps.prompt: We really have to do it

title: 7 · Yesterday
intro: The past tense is where Hebrew gets easier rather than harder: endings on a stem, and the "I" form ignores gender entirely.

steps.teach: "-ti" on the end = I did it. amar (said) → amarti.
Same ending, any verb. halach (went) → halachti.
"-nu" = we.
Now gender returns, but only outside the first person: he is the bare stem.
She adds -a.
"-ta" to a man, "-t" to a woman.

title: 8 · Whose: the ending that owns
intro: Hebrew can stick the owner onto the end of the thing owned. There's a longer way too, which is what people actually say for most words — both are worth having.

steps.teach: "sheli" = mine, and it follows the noun.
shelcha to a man, shelach to a woman.
shelo = his, shela = hers.
With close family, the ending sticks straight onto the word instead. ach = brother.
achot = sister.
Same trick for other people: achota = her sister.

title: 9 · Asking for things politely
intro: Israeli Hebrew is direct, and that isn't rudeness — but there is still a set of softeners, and they're short words rather than long constructions.

steps.teach: "efshar" = is it possible. The politeness engine, and it works before any infinitive.
Same shape, different verb.
"bevakasha" = please — and also "here you go" when you hand something over.
"slicha" opens a request to a stranger. It's both sorry and excuse me.
"ulai" = maybe, and it softens anything it touches.

steps.prompt: Excuse me, could I ask something?

title: 10 · Because, but, although
intro: Joining two thoughts. The good news: unlike its European neighbours, Hebrew never moves the verb around when you do this — the word order simply stays put.

steps.teach: "aval" = but.
steps.prompt: I want to come, but I don't have time
steps.answer: ani rotze lavo, aval ein li zman

steps.teach: "ki" = because. Nothing else changes — no verb sliding to the end.
Put it together.
steps.prompt: I can't come because I don't have time
steps.answer: ani lo yachol lavo ki ein li zman

steps.teach: "she-" = that, and it glues onto the next word rather than standing alone.
steps.prompt: I think that it's right (a man speaking)

steps.teach: "im" = if.
"lamrot she-" = although.

title: 11 · Tomorrow, and the future
intro: The future works the opposite way round to the past: instead of endings, it takes a prefix — and like the past, the "I" form doesn't care about gender.

steps.teach: "e-" on the front = I will. So lech (go) gives elech.
Same prefix on another verb.
"ni-" = we will.
And that's how Hebrew says "let's" — just the we-form.
steps.prompt: Come on, let's go (to a man)

steps.teach: "ti-" = you will, and it's also how you give an order.
To say don't, use "al" plus the future — never lo.
steps.prompt: Don't be like that (to a man)
I'll be right there (a man speaking)
steps.hint: Hebrew often uses the present for the immediate future

title: 12 · Sounding Israeli
intro: The words that carry tone. Several aren't Hebrew at all — Israeli speech borrows freely from Arabic and Yiddish, and these are the ones you'll hear within an hour of landing.

steps.teach: "yalla" is Arabic, and it means come on, let's go, hurry up, or fine then.
steps.prompt: Come on, let's go (to a man)

steps.teach: "beseder" = in order: fine, OK, agreed, alright.
"sababa" — also Arabic — is a warmer yes.
"tachles" is Yiddish: get to the point, bottom line, honestly.
"stam" = just because, no reason, never mind — or "only joking".
steps.hint: sho'elet if a woman is speaking

steps.teach: "nu?" is the impatient prompt: well? and? get on with it.

steps.prompt: Forget it, it's not worth it (to a man)

title: 13 · Reading without the vowels
intro: Hebrew leaves most vowels out of writing. That sounds impossible and isn't — you already do the same with English abbreviations. The trick is that consonants carry the meaning and vowels carry the grammar.

steps.teach: The three root letters carry the meaning. כ־ת־ב (k-t-v) is anything to do with writing.
Same three letters, different vowels, different word.
And again.
So the same written word can be two things, and the sentence decides. אמרתי לך is amarti lecha or amarti lach.
steps.prompt: I did tell you (to a woman)

steps.teach: Some letters do double duty as vowels. ו is v, o or u; י is y or i.
steps.hint: the ו here is the o

steps.teach: And the one rule worth having for reading aloud: ו meaning "and" is ve, essentially always in speech.
steps.hint: you'll hear u-mayim from a newsreader; not in conversation
